rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence fence and turns missing proof into gates instead of decorations. Its data angle says “what a non-peer-reviewed internal study can and cannot support,” which is exactly the posture an education reporter needs. B is useful, but “while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat” invents a market contrast the update did not supply; one lazy comparative claim in a headline is how a pitch gets kneecapped.
gaps_in_A: “Donors, not districts, are paying” overstates the payment mechanics. The update says Khanmigo is free to teachers and donor-funded; it does not prove districts pay nothing.
“Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning” is a little too causal for an internal, non-peer-reviewed study. Keep it closer to “regular users gained, by Khan’s own measure.”

“The district is joining the rollout, or its pilot results are part of what is being published now” leaves the customer-story angle with two different spines. Pick pilot evidence or rollout impact once a named district exists.
gaps_in_B: “one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments” is invented. The update gives 1 million additional students, not a category ranking.
“while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat” is an unsupported market claim. No competitor pricing or category economics were supplied.
“The prevailing optimism — AI tutoring boosts learning” inflates a caveated internal study into a public consensus. That is decoration, not grounding.
“the 30-district rollout is happening now” needs calendar proof. The update says rolling out, but not whether students use it immediately or in the next school year.
